tagline: Notion-style form builder with a generous free tier.
verdictSummary: A form builder — a field editor, public form pages, stored responses, CSV export — is a classic weekend build, and one of the cleanest yes entries here: there's enough mature prior art that this isn't even a hard weekend.
coreLoopDIY: An admin editor for building forms field by field, a public page per form that validates and stores responses, with CSV export and optional email/webhook notifications.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for low-friction form creation, removing the free-tier branding, and integrations that plug straight into other tools — not because a working form is hard to build.
notes: One of the cleanest yes products in the catalogue, with enough prior art to make this genuinely actionable, not just theoretically buildable.
prompt:
Build a personal form builder: an admin view (behind simple authentication, no need for full user accounts) for creating forms field by field — text, textarea, email, select, checkbox, file upload — with required flags and reordering. Each form gets its own public page with a clean single-column layout, client- and server-side validation, and basic spam defenses (a honeypot field plus a simple per-IP rate limit). Store every response in a database, with file uploads saved to disk under a size cap. Per form, support two optional notifications: email yourself on each new response, and POST the response as JSON to a webhook URL. An admin view per form: a sortable response table with CSV export.

Do not build partial-submission saving, conditional field logic, payment collection, or team workspaces — and skip a template gallery entirely; a form you built yourself is its own template. This is a personal tool, not a forms platform.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Tally forms?
faq.a: Not automatically — Tally doesn't offer a structured export of form definitions. Response data does export as CSV, so past submissions are safe; the form structure itself needs to be rebuilt, which for most forms is a few minutes of clicking.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: Yes for filling out a form — the public pages are fully responsive. The admin editor is usable on a phone but is built with a desktop layout in mind.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Hosting and a database, typically a few dollars a month — file uploads are the only thing that meaningfully grows storage costs over time.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Partial-submission recovery. Tally can save someone's progress on a long form if they leave and come back; this build only stores a completed submission, so an abandoned form is simply gone.
